name: Apollos
title: The Eloquent Preacher from Alexandria
summary: Apollos, a learned Jewish man with roots in the intellectual metropolis of Alexandria, distinguished himself as a powerful preacher and interpreter of Scripture in the early Christian movement. With his rhetorical gift and deep knowledge of the holy writings, he spoke boldly about Jesus, even though at first he knew only John's baptism. In Ephesus, Priscilla and Aquila expanded his understanding of God's way, and he then traveled to Achaia, where he strengthened the believers and publicly demonstrated from the Scriptures that Jesus is the Messiah. In Corinth, his ministry was so highly valued that divisions arose, which Paul addressed by reminding them that only God gives growth – regardless of who plants or waters. Paul refers to Apollos as a trusted brother and fellow worker, and his further missionary travels are confirmed in the letter to Titus.

keyEvents.title: Apollos Arrives in Ephesus
keyEvents.description: Apollos arrived in Ephesus as a learned man with thorough knowledge of the Scriptures and a fervent spirit, but he knew only the baptism of John.

keyEvents.title: Taught by Priscilla and Aquila
keyEvents.description: Priscilla and Aquila took Apollos aside and explained God's way to him more accurately, deepening his understanding of the gospel.

keyEvents.title: Ministry in Achaia
keyEvents.description: Apollos traveled to Achaia with a letter of recommendation from the brothers and was a great help to those who believed there, especially by publicly refuting the Jews, showing from the Scriptures that Jesus is the Messiah.

keyEvents.title: Divisions in Corinth
keyEvents.description: Paul addressed the division in the church at Corinth, where some said they belonged to Apollos, others to Paul or Cephas. Paul emphasized that both were servants who planted and watered, but it was God who gave the growth.

keyEvents.title: Apollos Encouraged to Visit Corinth
keyEvents.description: Paul referred to Apollos as a brother and fellow worker, encouraging him to visit Corinth again, though Apollos waited for a more suitable time.

keyEvents.title: Mentioned in the Letter to Titus
keyEvents.description: Paul asked Titus to help Apollos and Zenas on their journey and ensure they lacked nothing, showing Apollos' continued service in the early church.

versions.summary: Apollos was an educated Jewish man from Alexandria who became a prominent preacher in the early church. He was known for his eloquence, thorough knowledge of the Scriptures, and fervent spirit. After being instructed by Priscilla and Aquila, he became an important co-worker in proclaiming the gospel.
versions.title: The Eloquent Preacher
versions.reason: [major] The roles 'leader' and 'wise man' are imprecise for Apollos. He is primarily described as a preacher, teacher, and evangelist. He was eloquent and well-versed in the Scriptures, which makes the roles of 'preacher', 'teacher', and 'evangelist' more precise. 'Wise man' is not a standard designation used for Apollos in the New Testament.; [minor] The division in Corinth is first mentioned in 1 Cor 1:12, not only in 3:4-6. It could be useful to include a reference to 1 Cor 1:12 as well, since that is where the problem is first introduced.; [major] Footnotes are completely missing. A profile on Apollos should contain historical and linguistic footnotes about, among other things, Alexandria as a center of learning, the origin of the name Apollos, and the Alexandrian tradition of biblical interpretation.; [minor] The summary is good, but could briefly mention his ministry in Corinth and his relationship with Paul, which are central aspects of his biblical profile.

versions.summary: Apollos was a well-educated Jewish man from Alexandria who became a prominent preacher in the early church. He was known for his eloquence, thorough knowledge of the Scriptures, and his fervent spirit. After being more fully instructed by Priscilla and Aquila in Ephesus, he traveled to Achaia where he greatly helped the believers, especially by publicly refuting the Jews from the Scriptures. Apollos also worked in Corinth, where Paul described him as a fellow worker and equal servant in the gospel, emphasizing that while they planted and watered, it was God who gave the growth.
versions.title: The Eloquent Preacher from Alexandria
versions.reason:
[minor] The summary is very similar to version 1 (starting identically with "Apollos was a well-educated Jewish man from Alexandria who became a prominent preacher in the early..."). Since there is an earlier version with a score of 6 that starts the same way, the text should be rephrased to avoid repetition and improve quality.
[minor] The expression "equal servant in the gospel" is somewhat imprecise. Paul describes them as fellow workers with different tasks but does not use the word "equal" directly. A more nuanced formulation would have been better.
[major] Martin Luther lived in the 1500s and is not considered a church father. It is more correct to say that Luther was a reformer. Among those who have suggested Apollos as the author of Hebrews, there are actually Luther, but also others such as Origenes who discussed the question of authorship. The wording should be corrected so that Luther is not called a church father.
[minor] Apollos is explicitly described as "learned" (Greek: logios) in Acts 18:24. A role as "scribe" or "apologist" could also have been relevant, given his public defense of the faith against the Jews.
[minor] The event "Paul's fellow worker" has a somewhat imprecise title. The content is more about Apollos' independence and Paul's recommendation that he visit Corinth. A more descriptive title such as "Apollos encouraged to visit Corinth" could have been clearer.

footnotes.text: Alexandria in Egypt was one of the ancient world's most important centers of learning, with its famous library and large Jewish population. The Jewish philosopher Philo of Alexandria is perhaps the best-known representative of the Alexandrian Jewish intellectual tradition. That Apollos came from there explains his learning and rhetorical skills.

The name 'Apollos' is likely a shortened form of 'Apollonios,' a common Greek name derived from the god Apollo. This suggests a Hellenistic Jewish background, which was typical for Jews in the diaspora, especially in Alexandria.

The Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament) was produced in Alexandria, and Alexandrian Jews were known for their allegorical interpretive tradition. Apollos' thorough knowledge of the Scriptures was probably shaped by this tradition.

That Apollos knew only of 'John's baptism' (Acts 18:25) has been the subject of much theological discussion. It may mean that he had received teaching from disciples of John the Baptist who had spread into the diaspora, but had not yet received full instruction about Christian baptism and the gift of the Holy Spirit.

Several theologians throughout history, including the reformer Martin Luther, have proposed Apollos as a possible author of Hebrews, based on his Alexandrian background, eloquence, and thorough knowledge of Scripture. Already Origen (3rd century) discussed who wrote this letter. The hypothesis remains unconfirmed but is an interesting tradition.

The Greek word 'logios,' used about Apollos in Acts 18:24, can be translated as 'eloquent' or 'learned.' Both meanings fit well: Alexandria was known for its rhetorical training, and Apollos demonstrated both learning and speaking gifts in his service.
